nameStory: This coastal plant gets its 'sea-purslane' name from its succulent, fleshy leaves that resemble those of common purslane, but it lives by the ocean instead of in gardens. The 'annual' part distinguishes it from other sea-purslanes that live for multiple years. Like a salty cousin of the familiar garden purslane, it's perfectly adapted to life where land meets sea.
description: Annual Sea-purslane is a low-growing, sprawling plant that hugs sandy beaches and salt marshes along New England's coast. This succulent annual forms small mats or patches with thick, fleshy stems and leaves that help it survive in salty conditions. The plant stays fairly small, rarely getting taller than a few inches, but can spread outward to create small colonies. Its entire appearance screams 'beach plant' with its chunky, water-storing tissues and prostrate growth habit.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, succulent leaves that feel like little water balloons when gently squeezed - they're designed to store water and handle salt spray

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, sprawling mat-former that hugs the ground, rarely rising more than a few inches tall but spreading horizontally

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, inconspicuous flowers without showy petals - they're easy to miss and focus more on seed production than attracting pollinators

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Fleshy, somewhat translucent stems that feel firm and rubbery to the touch, often with a slightly reddish or pinkish tint

habitat: Look for Annual Sea-purslane on sandy beaches, in salt marshes, and along other coastal areas where salt spray is common. It thrives in the challenging environment where few other plants can survive - in sandy, salty soils that get regular doses of ocean spray. You'll typically find it growing alongside other salt-tolerant beach plants in the upper edges of tidal zones.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate as coastal temperatures warm, with tiny succulent seedlings appearing in sandy areas by late spring.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and produce their small, inconspicuous flowers during the warmest months when growth is most active.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to decline and set seed as cooler weather arrives, with the whole plant starting to deteriorate.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, plants die completely with first frost, leaving only seeds behind to start the cycle again next year.

funFact: Annual Sea-purslane's leaves can actually taste salty when you chew them - the plant literally stores salt in its tissues as a way to cope with its harsh coastal environment, making it like nature's own salt shaker!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other small, succulent coastal plants like glassworts or sea beans, but Annual Sea-purslane has broader, flatter leaves rather than the skinny, finger-like segments of glassworts. Remember: purslane leaves look more like tiny paddles, while glasswort looks more like green pickles.
contextualKnowledge: Despite sharing the 'purslane' name with the common garden weed, Annual Sea-purslane belongs to a completely different plant family (stone plants vs. purslane family) and is adapted for coastal rather than inland life. The name similarity comes from their shared succulent leaf appearance rather than close genetic relationship.
compareHints: Since Annual Sea-purslane is the only member of its genus found in New England, compare it to other members of the stone plant family, which are mostly tropical succulents. What makes this species special is its annual life cycle and its ability to thrive in temperate coastal conditions, unlike most of its warm-climate relatives. Most other stone plants are perennials from warmer regions, making this annual a unique cold-adapted member of the family.
